items.prompt: Pre-test, a guess is fine and nothing is marked against you. White to move. Tap every square the white king on e1 can step to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.

hints: Look at the squares around the king first. Which of them already hold White's own pieces?
A king can never move onto a square held by its own side. Cross out d2, e2 and f1.
Only two neighbouring squares are empty, one on each side of the king. Nothing black is near.
items.explain: The king on e1 touches five squares. A pawn stands on d2, a pawn on e2 and a bishop on f1, and a king cannot move onto its own side's pieces. That leaves d1 and f2.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the white king on b3 can step to. Watch your own pawn, the black king and the black knight.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.

hints: Give each neighbouring square a verdict: own piece, touches the black king, or attacked.
The pawn on a2 is yours. The black king on d4 covers c3 and c4. The knight on c6 jumps to b4.
Eight neighbours, four crossed out. The four left are on the a-file and the second and third ranks.
items.explain: The piece on b3 is a king. a2 holds its own pawn, c3 and c4 touch the black king on d4, and b4 is attacked by the knight on c6. The king can step to a3, a4, b2 and c2.

items.prompt: Nothing is labelled. Which piece stands on c4?

claims.statement: The piece on c4 is a bishop.

hints: Look at the shape of the piece, not at where it stands.
It is a long-range piece that moves only along diagonals.
Six names are offered. The one that slides along diagonals and is not a queen is the bishop.
items.explain: The piece on c4 is a white bishop. It slides along diagonals, here toward f7. Naming it first tells you which rule to use.

items.prompt: Which piece stands on g1? Name it before you do anything else.

claims.statement: The piece on g1 is a king.

hints: Look at the shape: this is the piece the whole game is about.
It sits in the corner, tucked behind three pawns, after castling.
Only one piece loses the game when it is lost: the king.
items.explain: The piece on g1 is the white king. It castled, so it now sits behind the f, g and h pawns.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on f4 can move to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.

hints: Say the piece's name first. Is it a king?
It is a knight: it jumps two squares one way and one square the other, and it may jump over pieces.
Eight jumps are possible from f4. One lands on White's own pawn, so that one is out. Captures are allowed.
items.explain: The piece on f4 is a knight, not a king. From f4 it can jump to d3, d5, e2, e6, g2, g6 and h5. The jump to h3 is blocked by its own pawn. The black pawns on e6 and g6 can be captured.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on e4 can move to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.

hints: Name the piece on e4. Then take its neighbours one at a time, attacker by attacker.
The rook is on the third rank, the bishop's diagonal runs to e3, the knight jumps to e5, the pawn covers d5 and the black king covers d3 and e3.
The squares on the e-file and to its left are all covered. The free ones are on the f-file, and one f-square is on the rook's rank.
items.explain: The rook on a3 attacks d3, e3 and f3. The bishop on b6 attacks d4 and e3. The pawn on c6 attacks d5, the knight on d7 attacks e5, and the black king on d2 attacks d3 and e3. The king can step only to f4 and f5.

items.prompt: The black rook checks along the fourth rank. Can the white king step to f4, the square behind it on the same line? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: This move is not legal.
White is in check.

hints: Which line is the check on? Is f4 on that line?
The rook sees along the fourth rank. The king is standing in the way, but only until it moves.
After the king steps to f4 it is still on the rook's rank, with nothing between them.
items.explain: The rook on b4 attacks along the fourth rank, and the king on e4 is the only piece in the way. If the king stepped to f4 it would still be on that line, so the rook would attack it there. The move is illegal.

items.prompt: White to move, in check from the bishop. Tap every square the white king can step to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.

hints: Find the bishop's diagonal. Which two squares beside the king lie on it?
The diagonal runs from b6 through c5 and d4. Remember the square behind the king.
Six neighbouring squares are free. Cross out c5 and e3, the two on the diagonal.
items.explain: The bishop on b6 attacks along the diagonal through c5 to the king on d4. c5 is on that diagonal in front of the king and e3 is on it behind. The other six neighbours are free: c3, c4, d3, d5, e4 and e5.

items.prompt: White to move. Can the king on f4 take the knight on e5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: This move is not legal.
One black piece defends the knight.

hints: Who could take back on e5 if the king captured?
Look at the squares around e5, not only the long lines.
The black king on e6 touches e5.
items.explain: The black king on e6 stands next to e5 and so defends the knight. If the white king took, it would stand next to the black king, which is not allowed.

items.prompt: White to move. Can the king on e4 take the knight on d5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: This move is not legal.
One black piece defends the knight.

hints: Who could take back on d5 if the king captured?
Look at every line that reaches d5, even one that starts far away.
The bishop on a2 looks along a2-b3-c4-d5. Nothing stands in between, so it defends d5.
items.explain: The bishop on a2 looks along its diagonal through b3 and c4 and defends d5. If the king took the knight it would stand on an attacked square, so the capture is illegal.

items.prompt: White to move. Can the king on e4 take the knight on d5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: This move is legal.
No black piece defends the knight.

hints: Who could take back on d5 if the king captured?
Look at every line that reaches d5. Is each one clear all the way?
The black pawn on c4 stands on the bishop's diagonal and blocks it.
items.explain: The bishop on a2 would defend d5, but the black pawn on c4 stands in its way. Nothing else attacks d5, so the king may take the knight.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on d4 can move to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.

hints: Name the piece. Then look at the two black pieces next to it: is either one capturable?
The knight on d3 is defended by the rook on d2. The pawn on e4 has no defender.
The king can capture on e4 but not on d3. The squares c5 and e5 are covered by the knight.
items.explain: The knight on d3 is defended by the rook on d2 below it, so the king cannot take it. The pawn on e4 has no defender, so the king can take it. The knight also covers c5 and e5. The king can go to c3, c4, d5, e3 and e4.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on d4 can move to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.
The king cannot take the defended knight.
One black piece defends the knight on c3.

hints: Name the piece. Then ask of the knight next to it: does anything defend it?
Exactly one piece differs from the working position. Find it.
A black pawn stands on b4, and a pawn attacks the squares diagonally in front of it.
items.explain: The piece on d4 is a king. The pawn on b4 defends the knight on c3, so the king cannot take it. It can step to c4, d3, e3 and e5.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the piece on d4 can move to. Four black pieces watch it.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the piece can move to.

hints: Name the piece. Then cross out squares one attacker at a time.
The rook covers the fifth rank, the bishop and knight each cover squares below the king, and the pawn covers e3.
Six squares fall. The two left are on opposite sides of the king.
items.explain: The piece on d4 is a king. The rook on f5 covers d5, c5 and e5. The bishop covers c4 and d3. The knight covers c4 and d3 as well. The pawn on f4 covers e3. That leaves c3 and e4.

items.prompt: White to move. Can the king on e4 take the knight on d5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: This move is not legal.
One black piece defends the knight.

hints: Who could take back on d5 if the king captured?
Look at every line that reaches d5. A pinned piece may be the one.
The bishop on g8 is pinned to its king by the rook, but a pinned piece still guards its squares.
items.explain: The bishop on g8 is pinned by the rook on a8, yet it still attacks d5 through f7 and e6. A king may never step onto a square an enemy piece attacks, pinned or not. The capture is illegal.
